claim: Caulobacter crescentus is a polarized alpha-proteobacterium.
source: Our forward genetic selection unearthed the Krebs cycle enzyme citrate synthase (CitA) as a checkpoint regulator controlling the G1→S transition in the polarized alpha-proteobacterium Caulobacter crescentus, a model for cell cycle regulation and asymmetric cell division.
evidence: Stated directly in the abstract as a description of the organism.

claim: Caulobacter crescentus is a model for cell cycle regulation and asymmetric cell division.
source: Our forward genetic selection unearthed the Krebs cycle enzyme citrate synthase (CitA) as a checkpoint regulator controlling the G1→S transition in the polarized alpha-proteobacterium Caulobacter crescentus, a model for cell cycle regulation and asymmetric cell division.
evidence: Stated directly in the abstract and supported by citation in the introduction.

claim: CitA is a Krebs cycle enzyme citrate synthase.
source: Our forward genetic selection unearthed the Krebs cycle enzyme citrate synthase (CitA) as a checkpoint regulator controlling the G1→S transition in the polarized alpha-proteobacterium Caulobacter crescentus, a model for cell cycle regulation and asymmetric cell division.
evidence: Stated in the abstract and confirmed by experimental data showing citrate synthase activity.

claim: CitA functions as a checkpoint regulator controlling the G1→S transition.
source: Our forward genetic selection unearthed the Krebs cycle enzyme citrate synthase (CitA) as a checkpoint regulator controlling the G1→S transition in the polarized alpha-proteobacterium Caulobacter crescentus, a model for cell cycle regulation and asymmetric cell division.
evidence: Stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data showing G1 accumulation in citA mutants.

claim: Loss of CitA promotes the accumulation of active CtrA.
source: We find that loss of CitA promotes the accumulation of active CtrA, an essential cell cycle transcriptional regulator that maintains cells in G1-phase, provided that the (p)ppGpp alarmone is present.
evidence: Stated in the abstract and supported by immunoblotting and Phos-tag PAGE data.

claim: CtrA is an essential cell cycle transcriptional regulator that maintains cells in G1-phase.
source: We find that loss of CitA promotes the accumulation of active CtrA, an essential cell cycle transcriptional regulator that maintains cells in G1-phase, provided that the (p)ppGpp alarmone is present.
evidence: Stated in the abstract and supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: The effect of CitA loss on CtrA accumulation requires the presence of (p)ppGpp alarmone.
source: We find that loss of CitA promotes the accumulation of active CtrA, an essential cell cycle transcriptional regulator that maintains cells in G1-phase, provided that the (p)ppGpp alarmone is present.
evidence: Stated in the abstract and supported by data showing that ΔspoT or ΔptsP mutations suppress the citA phenotype.

claim: The enzymatic activity of CitA is dispensable for CtrA control.
source: The enzymatic activity of CitA is dispensable for CtrA control, and functional citrate synthase paralogs cannot replace CitA in promoting S-phase entry.
evidence: Stated in the abstract and supported by data showing that catalytically inactive CitA variants (CitAH303W and CitAH303A) restore normal cell cycle progression.

claim: Functional citrate synthase paralogs cannot replace CitA in promoting S-phase entry.
source: The enzymatic activity of CitA is dispensable for CtrA control, and functional citrate synthase paralogs cannot replace CitA in promoting S-phase entry.
evidence: Stated in the abstract and supported by complementation experiments showing CitB and GltA cannot rescue the citA mutant phenotype.

claim: CitA functions as a moonlighting enzyme to link central energy metabolism with S-phase entry.
source: Our evidence suggests that CitA was appropriated specifically to function as a moonlighting enzyme to link central energy metabolism with S-phase entry.
evidence: Stated in the abstract as an interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: Moonlighting enzymes are metabolic enzymes appropriated for regulatory functions instead of or in addition to their normal enzymatic functions.
source: Such metabolic enzymes, often enzyme paralogs, that are appropriated for regulatory functions instead of or in addition to their normal enzymatic functions have been called moonlighting or trigger enzymes.
evidence: Stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Moonlighting enzymes are ideal coupling factors to coordinate regulatory changes in response to metabolic fluctuations.
source: Their enzymatic ancestry makes them ideal coupling factors to coordinate regulatory changes in response to metabolic fluctuations (Commichau and Stülke, 2015; Huberts and van der Klei, 2010), for example in bacterial cell cycle control.
evidence: Stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Caulobacter crescentus is the preeminent model for elucidating fundamental cell cycle control mechanisms.
source: The synchronizable α-proteobacterium Caulobacter crescentus is the preeminent model for elucidating fundamental cell cycle control mechanisms (Hallez et al., 2017).
evidence: Stated in the introduction with supporting citation.

claim: Cell division in C. crescentus is asymmetric and yields two dissimilar daughter cells.
source: Cell division in C. crescentus is asymmetric and thus yields two dissimilar daughter cells.
evidence: Stated in the introduction as established knowledge about the organism.

claim: One daughter cell is a stalked and capsulated S-phase cell that replicates its genome before dividing.
source: One daughter cell is a stalked and capsulated S-phase cell that replicates its genome before dividing.
evidence: Stated in the introduction as established knowledge about the organism.

claim: The other daughter cell is a piliated and flagellated dispersal (swarmer) cell that resides in the non-replicative and non-dividing G1-phase.
source: The other is a piliated and flagellated dispersal (swarmer) cell that resides in the non-replicative and non-dividing G1-phase (Figure 1A).
evidence: Stated in the introduction and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: The old pole of the stalked cell features a cylindrical extension of the cell envelope.
source: The old pole of the stalked cell features a cylindrical extension of the cell envelope, whereas that of the swarmer cell is decorated with a single flagellum and several adhesive pili.
evidence: Stated in the introduction as established knowledge about cell morphology.

claim: The old pole of the swarmer cell is decorated with a single flagellum and several adhesive pili.
source: The old pole of the stalked cell features a cylindrical extension of the cell envelope, whereas that of the swarmer cell is decorated with a single flagellum and several adhesive pili.
evidence: Stated in the introduction as established knowledge about cell morphology.

claim: The placement and construction of organelles at the correct cell pole is dictated by the prior recruitment of polar scaffolding proteins, including TipN and PodJ.
source: The placement and construction of organelles at the correct cell pole is dictated by the prior recruitment of polar scaffolding proteins, including the TipN and PodJ coiled-coil proteins (Figure 1A; Hinz et al., 2003; Huitema et al., 2006; Lam et al., 2006; Viollier et al., 2002) and the PopZ polar organizer (Bowman et al., 2008; Ebersbach et al., 2008).
evidence: Stated in the introduction with supporting citations and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: PopZ is a polar organizer involved in organelle placement.
source: The placement and construction of organelles at the correct cell pole is dictated by the prior recruitment of polar scaffolding proteins, including the TipN and PodJ coiled-coil proteins (Figure 1A; Hinz et al., 2003; Huitema et al., 2006; Lam et al., 2006; Viollier et al., 2002) and the PopZ polar organizer (Bowman et al., 2008; Ebersbach et al., 2008).
evidence: Stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Polarity determinants affect progression of the cell division cycle.
source: As polar remodeling occurs as function of the cell cycle, it is not surprising that polarity determinants also affect progression of the cell division cycle (reviewed inby Bergé and Viollier, 2018).
evidence: Stated in the introduction with supporting citation.

claim: Tn insertions in cpdR, rcdA, and popA are underrepresented in ΔtipN cells compared to WT cells.
source: This analysis revealed Tn insertions in cpdR, rcdA or popA genes that are underrepresented in ∆tipN cells when compared with WT cells (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: Stated in the results and supported by Tn-Seq data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: cpdR, rcdA, and popA encode a hierarchical proteolytic adaptor cascade that coordinates delivery of substrates to ClpXP protease.
source: These three genes encode a hierarchical proteolytic adaptor cascade that coordinates the delivery of a range of substrates, including CtrA, to the ClpXP protease for proteolytic removal during the G1→S transition (Duerig et al., 2009; Iniesta et al., 2006; Joshi et al., 2015; Joshi and Chien, 2016; McGrath et al., 2006).
evidence: Stated in the results with supporting citations.

claim: Tn insertions in tipN are underrepresented in ΔcpdR cells compared to WT cells.
source: A converse Tn-Seq comparison between WT and ∆cpdR cells also revealed an underrepresentation of Tn insertions in the tipN gene (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B, Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: Stated in the results and supported by Tn-Seq data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: ΔtipN; ΔcpdR, ΔtipN; ΔrcdA, and ΔtipN; ΔpopA double mutants exhibit a reduction in viability by three orders of magnitude.
source: To confirm the genetic relationship between tipN and cpdR, rcdA or popA, we created double mutants by introducing the ∆cpdR, ∆rcdA or ∆popA mutations into ∆tipN cells and found that all of the resulting double mutants exhibit a reduction in viability by three orders of magnitude on a logarithmic scale, as determined by efficiency of plating (EOP) assays (Figure 1C; Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: Stated in the results and supported by EOP assay data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and D.

claim: ΔtipN; ΔcpdR double mutant cells are 70% more elongated on average than WT and single mutant cells.
source: Examination of ∆tipN; ∆cpdR double mutant cells by phase-contrast microscopy showed that they are 70% more elongated on average than WT and ∆cpdR, ∆rcdA or ∆popA single mutant cells (Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1E and F).
evidence: Stated in the results and supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1E and F.

claim: ΔtipN; ΔcpdR double mutant cells show a massive reduction in the number of G1-phase cells and an increase in cells with multiple chromosomes.
source: Flow cytometry analysis of exponentially growing ∆tipN; ∆cpdR double mutant cells using a fluorescence activated cell sorter (FACS) revealed a massive reduction in the number of G1-phase cells and an increase in the frequency of cells with multiple (>2) chromosomes compared to WT, whereas ∆cpdR and ∆tipN single mutants only showed a slight decrease in the G1 population (Figure 1D).
evidence: Stated in the results and supported by FACS data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: ΔtipN; ΔrcdA and ΔtipN; ΔpopA double mutants show accumulation of elongated cells and reduction in G1-phase cells.
source: Importantly, the ∆tipN; ∆rcdA and ∆tipN; ∆popA double mutants show a similar accumulation of elongated cells and reduction in the number of G1-phase cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E and F).
evidence: Stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E and F.

claim: The proteolytic adaptors promote efficient cell cycle progression in cells that lack TipN.
source: Thus, the proteolytic adaptors promote efficient cell cycle progression in cells that lack TipN.
evidence: Stated as a conclusion in the results based on the genetic interaction data.

claim: A reduction in the proportion of G1 cells is often correlated with reduced activity or abundance of CtrA.
source: A reduction in the proportion of G1 cells is often correlated with reduced activity or abundance of CtrA, the principal G1-phase transcriptional regulator.
evidence: Stated in the results as established knowledge.

claim: GFP fluorescence intensity from the pilA::PpilA-GFP reporter is strongly reduced in ΔtipN; ΔcpdR double mutant cells.
source: In agreement with the FACS profiles shown in Figure 1E, GFP fluorescence intensity is only slightly lower in ∆cpdR cells than in WT cells, but clearly reduced in ∆tipN cells. Importantly, a further strong decrease in GFP fluorescence is observed in ∆tipN; ∆cpdR double mutant cells, indicating a strong downregulation in CtrA-dependent reporter activity.
evidence: Stated in the results and supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Transcription from the pilA::PpilA-nptII reporter is strongly reduced in ΔtipN; ΔcpdR double mutant cells.
source: Likewise, transcription from a reporter in which PpilA is fused to the promoter-less nptII gene (conferring resistance to kanamycin) at the pilA locus (pilA::PpilA-nptII) is strongly reduced in ∆tipN; ∆cpdR double mutant cells when compared to WT cells, precluding growth on plates containing 20 µg/mL kanamycin (Figure 2B).
evidence: Stated in the results and supported by growth assay data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Cells that lack both TipN and CpdR suffer from an insufficiency of CtrA.
source: We conclude that cells that lack both TipN and CpdR suffer from an insufficiency of CtrA.
evidence: Stated as a conclusion in the results based on reporter assay data.

claim: Inactivation of CpdR, RcdA, or PopA should enhance CtrA abundance in ΔtipN cells.
source: Paradoxically, inactivation of CpdR, RcdA or PopA should enhance CtrA abundance in ∆tipN cells, since the proteolytic removal of CtrA at the G1→S transition should be blocked in the absence of each of these adaptors.
evidence: Stated as a logical inference based on known function of the proteolytic adaptors.

claim: An inhibitor of the CtrA pathway that is degraded by the CpdR-RcdA-PopA pathway accumulates in the absence of CpdR.
source: We therefore reasoned that another, indirect, effect underlies the crippled CtrA activity in ∆tipN ; ∆cpdR cells. It could be that this effect is mediated by an inhibitor of the CtrA pathway that is also degraded by the CpdR-RcdA-PopA pathway, which would accumulate in the absence of CpdR.
evidence: Stated as a hypothesis in the results to explain the paradoxical observation.

claim: Tn insertions in kidO are increased 19-fold in ΔtipN; ΔcpdR double mutant cells versus WT or single mutant cells.
source: We sought to uncover this gene by comparative Tn-Seq analyses in ∆tipN; ∆cpdR double mutant cells versus WT or ∆tipN and ∆cpdR single mutant cells, and we found a 19-fold increase in Tn insertions in the kidO gene (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A, Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: Stated in the results and supported by Tn-Seq data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: KidO is a bifunctional oxidoreductase-like negative regulator of cell division and the CtrA pathway.
source: KidO is a bifunctional oxidoreductase-like negative regulator of cell division and the CtrA pathway (Radhakrishnan et al., 2010).
evidence: Stated in the results with supporting citation.

claim: KidO is degraded during the G1→S transition by CpdR/RcdA/PopA adaptor-primed ClpXP.
source: Akin to CtrA, KidO is degraded during the G1→S transition by (CpdR/RcdA/PopA) adaptor-primed ClpXP.
evidence: Stated in the results based on cited literature.

claim: KidO is stabilized in cells lacking CpdR, RcdA, or PopA.
source: As KidO is stabilized in cells lacking CpdR, RcdA or PopA (Radhakrishnan et al., 2010), we asked whether the stabilization of KidO confers the cell defect of ∆tipN; ∆cpdR cells.
evidence: Stated in the results with supporting citation.

claim: Expression of non-degradable KidO (kidOAA::DD) in ΔtipN cells causes high filamentation and cells with more than two chromosomes.
source: The resulting ∆tipN xylX::kidOAA::DD cells are highly filamentous, even without induction of the xylX promoter by xylose: with more than two chromosomes recapitulating the phenotype of the ∆tipN; ∆cpdR double mutant cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Stated in the results and supported by FACS and microscopy data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Deletion of kidO restores a near WT cell division phenotype to ΔtipN; ΔcpdR cells.
source: Conversely, an in-frame deletion in kidO (∆kidO) restores a near WT cell division phenotype to ∆tipN; ∆cpdR cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Stated in the results and supported by FACS data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Stabilization of KidO strongly impairs progression of the cell division cycle in cells lacking TipN.
source: Taken together, these experiments support the conclusion that stabilization of KidO strongly impairs progression of the cell division cycle in cells lacking TipN.
evidence: Stated as a conclusion in the results based on genetic experiments.

claim: A Tn insertion in citA was isolated that restores PpilA activity in ΔtipN; ΔcpdR cells.
source: Among several isolated mutants, we found one mutant harboring a Tn insertion in the middle of the CCNA_01983 (henceforth citA) gene, whose gene product is annotated as a type II citrate synthase (PRK05614).
evidence: Stated in the results describing the genetic screen.

claim: The citA::Tn mutation confers kanamycin resistance to ΔtipN; ΔcpdR; pilA::PpilA-nptII reporter cells.
source: After confirming by backcrossing that the citA::Tn mutation did indeed confer kanamycin resistance to ∆tipN; ∆cpdR; pilA::PpilA-nptII reporter cells, we engineered an in-frame deletion of citA (∆citA) and found that this mutation also supports growth of ∆tipN; ∆cpdR; pilA::PpilA-nptII reporter cells on kanamycin plates, indicating that inactivation of citA augments PpilA activity (Figure 2B).
evidence: Stated in the results and supported by growth assay data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The citA::Tn and ΔcitA mutations correct the abnormal cell size distribution of ΔtipN; ΔcpdR double mutant cells.
source: Moreover, the citA::Tn or the ∆citA mutations both correct the abnormal cell size distribution (cell filamentation) and augment the G1 population of ∆tipN; ∆cpdR double mutant cells (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Stated in the results and supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The citA::Tn and ΔcitA mutations augment the G1 population of ΔtipN; ΔcpdR double mutant cells.
source: Moreover, the citA::Tn or the ∆citA mutations both correct the abnormal cell size distribution (cell filamentation) and augment the G1 population of ∆tipN; ∆cpdR double mutant cells (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Stated in the results and supported by FACS data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Inactivation of citA causes a strong increase of PpilA activity and promotes accumulation of G1 cells in the absence of TipN and CpdR.
source: In sum, inactivation of citA gene causes a strong increase of PpilA activity and promotes the accumulation of G1 cells in the joint absence of TipN and CpdR.
evidence: Stated as a summary conclusion in the results based on reporter and FACS data.

claim: C. crescentus CitA has 65% amino acid identity to E. coli GltA citrate synthase.
source: C. crescentus CitA has 65% amino acid identity to the GltA citrate synthase from Escherichia coli K12 (strain MG1655) and 32% identity to CitA from Bacillus subtilis (strain 168).
evidence: Stated in the results based on sequence analysis.

claim: C. crescentus CitA has 32% amino acid identity to B. subtilis CitA.
source: C. crescentus CitA has 65% amino acid identity to the GltA citrate synthase from Escherichia coli K12 (strain MG1655) and 32% identity to CitA from Bacillus subtilis (strain 168).
evidence: Stated in the results based on sequence analysis.

claim: C. crescentus CitA complements glutamate auxotrophy in E. coli ΔgltA cells.
source: As expected, E. coli ∆gltA cells harboring the empty vector were unable to grow in (M9) minimal medium without glutamate, but ∆gltA cells grew well in the presence of either the gltA- or the citA-expression plasmid (Figure 3B).
evidence: Stated in the results and supported by growth assay data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: C. crescentus citA encodes a functional citrate synthase.
source: Thus, C. crescentus citA encodes a functional citrate synthase.
evidence: Stated as a conclusion in the results based on heterologous complementation data.

claim: Metabolomic profiling of citA::Tn and ΔcitA cells did not show significant differences in many TCA cycle metabolites including citrate and isocitrate compared to WT.
source: Surprisingly, these metabolomic analyses did not show any significant difference in many TCAs such as citrate and isocitrate when comparing WT and citA mutant cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Stated in the results and supported by LC-MS data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: There is a small increase in acetyl-CoA levels in citA mutant cells.
source: An indication that TCA cycle flux is nevertheless affected in the absence of CitA comes from the observation that there is a small increase in the levels of acetyl-CoA, as would be expected for citrate synthase mutant cells (Figure 3C).
evidence: Stated in the results and supported by LC-MS data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: CitA is not essential for viability of C. crescentus cells on PYE.
source: Unlike other TCA cycle enzymes, CitA is not essential for the viability of C. crescentus cells on PYE (Christen et al., 2011).
evidence: Stated in the results with supporting citation.

claim: C. crescentus encodes two other putative citrate synthase genes: citB (CCNA_03757) and citC (CCNA_03758).
source: Indeed, BLAST searches revealed the presence of two other putative citrate synthase genes: CCNA_03757 and CCNA_03758 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A) (henceforth citB and citC, respectively), which were also annotated as non-essential for viability on PYE (Christen et al., 2011).
evidence: Stated in the results based on BLAST searches and cited Tn-Seq data.

claim: CitB has 30% amino acid identity to C. crescentus CitA.
source: The citB and citC genes encode proteins with 30% and 32% identity to CitA from C. crescentus, 30% and 33% identity to GltA from E. coli K12 (MG1655), and 37% and 32% identity to CitA from Bacillus subtilis strain 168.
evidence: Stated in the results based on sequence analysis.

claim: CitC has 32% amino acid identity to C. crescentus CitA.
source: The citB and citC genes encode proteins with 30% and 32% identity to CitA from C. crescentus, 30% and 33% identity to GltA from E. coli K12 (MG1655), and 37% and 32% identity to CitA from Bacillus subtilis strain 168.
evidence: Stated in the results based on sequence analysis.

claim: CitB complements glutamate auxotrophy in E. coli ΔgltA cells.
source: We therefore tested the ability of citB and citC to support citrate synthase function by heterologous complementation of the glutamate auxotrophy of E. coli ∆gltA cells on minimal medium lacking glutamate, and found that expression of CitB, but not CitC, supported growth (Figure 3B).
evidence: Stated in the results and supported by growth assay data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: CitC does not complement glutamate auxotrophy in E. coli ΔgltA cells.
source: We therefore tested the ability of citB and citC to support citrate synthase function by heterologous complementation of the glutamate auxotrophy of E. coli ∆gltA cells on minimal medium lacking glutamate, and found that expression of CitB, but not CitC, supported growth (Figure 3B).
evidence: Stated in the results and supported by growth assay data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: C. crescentus citB encodes a functional citrate synthase.
source: Thus, C. crescentus citB also encodes a functional citrate synthase and citA mutants are probably able to grow on PYE because of residual citrate synthase activity conferred by CitB.
evidence: Stated as a conclusion in the results based on heterologous complementation data.

claim: citA mutants are able to grow on PYE because of residual citrate synthase activity conferred by CitB.
source: Thus, C. crescentus citB also encodes a functional citrate synthase and citA mutants are probably able to grow on PYE because of residual citrate synthase activity conferred by CitB.
evidence: Stated as an inference in the results based on the presence of functional CitB.

claim: ΔcitBC cells do not accept citA::Tn or ΔcitA::pNPTS138 by generalized transduction.
source: Unlike WT cells, ∆citBC cells do not accept citA::Tn or ∆citA::pNPTS138 generalized transducing particles (Figure 3D), but accept generalized transducing particles harboring another genomic locus marked with either the gentamycin or the kanamycin resistance gene with efficiency similar to that of WT cells.
evidence: Stated in the results and supported by transduction data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: C. crescentus encodes at least two functional citrate synthases, one of which is absolutely required for growth on PYE.
source: We conclude that C. crescentus encodes at least two functional citrate synthases, one of which is absolutely required for growth on PYE.
evidence: Stated as a conclusion in the results based on transduction experiments showing synthetic lethality.

claim: Absence of CitA leads to a slow growth phenotype in PYE.
source: First, EOP assays and growth curve measurements indicate that the absence of CitA leads to a slow growth phenotype in PYE and that CitA is required for growth on minimal M2G medium (Figure 4A).
evidence: Stated in the results and supported by growth assay data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: CitA is required for growth on minimal M2G medium.
source: First, EOP assays and growth curve measurements indicate that the absence of CitA leads to a slow growth phenotype in PYE and that CitA is required for growth on minimal M2G medium (Figure 4A).
evidence: Stated in the results and supported by growth assay data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: ΔcitA cells are shorter and narrower than WT cells.
source: Phase contrast microscopy of citA::Tn or ∆citA mutant cells revealed that ∆citA cells are shorter and narrower than WT cells (areas of 0.42 ± 0.009 µm and 0.43 ± 0.007 µm, respectively, for the citA::Tn and ∆citA compared to 0.69 ± 0.01 µm for WT cells; Figure 4B), perhaps because they spend more time in the non-growing G1 phase.
evidence: Stated in the results and supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: 68.3% of citA::Tn cells and 69.3% of ΔcitA cells reside in G1 phase compared to 36.1% of WT cells.
source: Indeed, FACS profiles revealed a strong increase in the G1-phase population in the absence of CitA: 68.3 ± 1.25% and 69.3 ± 1.22 of citA::Tn and ∆citA cells, respectively, reside in G1 phase compared to 36.1 ± 0.6% of WT cells (Figure 4B).
evidence: Stated in the results and supported by FACS data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The citA mutant phenotypes are not corrected by addition of exogenous glutamine.
source: Importantly, these phenotypes of citA mutant cells cannot be corrected by the addition of exogenous glutamine and, therefore, are not related to glutamine auxotrophy.
evidence: Stated in the results and supported by growth and FACS data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: The citA mutant phenotypes are not corrected by complementation with citB or gltA.
source: The citA mutant phenotypes are not corrected by complementation of citA mutant cells with a multi-copy plasmid harboring C. crescentus citB (pMT335-citB) or E. coli gltA (pMT335-gltA), arguing that these functions probably depend on the presence of the CitA protein rather than on citrate synthase enzymatic activity (Figure 4C).
evidence: Stated in the results and supported by FACS data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The citA mutant phenotypes are corrected when WT citA is expressed in trans.
source: However, these deficiencies are corrected when a WT copy of citA is expressed in trans on a multi-copy plasmid (pMT335-citA) (Figure 4C).
evidence: Stated in the results and supported by FACS data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: CitA promotes the G1→S transition, a function that other citrate synthases such as CitB and GltA cannot provide.
source: Thus, CitA promotes the G1→S transition, a function that other citrate synthases such as CitB and GltA cannot provide.
evidence: Stated as a conclusion in the results based on complementation experiments.

claim: CitAH303W and CitAH303A variants have lost enzymatic activity.
source: As expected, expression of the CitAH303W or CitAH303A variant in E. coli ∆gltA cells no longer correct the glutamate auxotrophy on minimal medium, as determined by EOP assays (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C). Immunoblotting using polyclonal antibodies to CitA revealed that these variants are produced to the same levels as WT CitA (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D). We therefore conclude that CitAH303W and CitAH303A have lost enzymatic activity.
evidence: Stated as a conclusion in the results based on complementation assays and immunoblotting data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C and D.

claim: Catalytically inactive CitA variants (CitAH303W and CitAH303A) restore normal FACS profile and cell size distribution to ΔcitA cells.
source: When these variants are expressed in C. crescentus ∆citA mutant cells to similar levels as WT CitA (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E), a normal FACS profile and cell size distribution is observed by phase-contrast microscopy (Figure 4D).
evidence: Stated in the results and supported by FACS and microscopy data shown in Figure 4D and immunoblotting data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E.

claim: The catalytic activity of CitA is dispensable for its developmental function.
source: As these results show that the catalytic activity of CitA is dispensable for its developmental function, CitA must fulfill a specific regulatory role in promoting the G1→S transition.
evidence: Stated as a conclusion in the results based on experiments with catalytically inactive CitA variants.

claim: WT G1 cells initiate DNA replication 30 minutes after release into PYE.
source: FACS profiles revealed that WT G1 cells initiate DNA replication 30 minutes after their release into PYE, whereas citA::Tn or ∆citA G1 cells do not enter S-phase before 90 minutes after their release into PYE (Figure 4—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: Stated in the results and supported by FACS data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1G.

claim: citA::Tn or ΔcitA G1 cells do not enter S-phase before 90 minutes after release into PYE.
source: FACS profiles revealed that WT G1 cells initiate DNA replication 30 minutes after their release into PYE, whereas citA::Tn or ∆citA G1 cells do not enter S-phase before 90 minutes after their release into PYE (Figure 4—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: Stated in the results and supported by FACS data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1G.

claim: A fraction of citA::Tn or ΔcitA cells remain in G1 phase, with only approximately half entering S-phase.
source: We also discovered that a fraction of citA::Tn or ∆citA cells remain in G1 phase, with only approximately half entering S-phase.
evidence: Stated in the results based on FACS data.

claim: In synchronized WT G1 cells, ~80% have a duplicated GFP-ParB focus after 40 minutes.
source: In synchronized WT G1 cells expressing ParB-GFP, we observed a single, polarly localized Cori, represented by a single GFP-ParB focus. After 40 minutes, ~80% (n = 39) of the cells have a duplicated GFP-ParB focus, one of which is segregated to the opposite pole.
evidence: Stated in the results and supported by time-lapse microscopy data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: In citA::Tn or ΔcitA G1 cells, a duplicated GFP-ParB focus only appeared in some cells after 100 minutes.
source: By contrast, in citA::Tn (n = 35) or ∆citA (n = 29) G1 cells, a duplicated GFP-ParB focus only appeared in some cells after 100 minutes.
evidence: Stated in the results and supported by time-lapse microscopy data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: After 260 minutes, ~60% of citA mutant cells still exhibit only one GFP-ParB focus.
source: Importantly, we noticed that even after 260 minutes, ~60% of the population still exhibit only one GFP-ParB focus.
evidence: Stated in the results and supported by time-lapse microscopy data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: A large fraction of the citA mutant population remains in G1-phase and only part enters S-phase.
source: Thus, a large fraction of the population remains in G1-phase and only part of the citA mutant population enters S-phase.
evidence: Stated as a conclusion in the results based on time-lapse microscopy data.

claim: citA G1 cells harbor a long stalk.
source: While chromosome duplication is delayed, citA G1 cells harbor a long stalk, as indicated by live-cell fluorescence imaging with the stalk marker StpX-GFP (Hughes et al., 2010), which coincides with the presence of a SpmX-mCherry focus, a marker of the stalked pole (Figure 4F).
evidence: Stated in the results and supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Polar remodeling and chromosome replication are uncoupled in the absence of CitA.
source: Knowing that SpmX is normally absent from the G1 cells, we hypothesized that polar remodeling and chromosome replication might be uncoupled in the absence of CitA (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Stated as a hypothesis in the results and supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Inactivation of citA augments activity of CtrA-activated promoters.
source: As inactivation of citA augments PpilA activity, we hypothesized that the citA mutation elevates CtrA activity and/or abundance. To test this hypothesis, we asked whether the activity of other CtrA-activated promoters is also elevated in ∆citA cells compared to WT cells. LacZ-based promoter probe assays indeed revealed elevated activity of CtrA-dependent promoters (Figure 5A).
evidence: Stated in the results and supported by β-galactosidase assay data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Levels of phosphorylated CtrA (CtrA~P) in ΔcitA cells are elevated relative to WT cells.
source: To explore whether loss of CitA alters the levels of active CtrA, we used immunoblotting of Phos-tag PAGE to confirm that the levels of phosphorylated CtrA (CtrA ~P) in extracts of ∆citA cells are elevated relative to those in WT cell extracts (Figure 5B and C).
evidence: Stated in the results and supported by Phos-tag PAGE immunoblotting data shown in Figure 5B and C.

claim: CtrA is more stable in ΔcitA cells than in WT cells.
source: This result prompted us to investigate whether this increase of CtrA steady-state levels was caused by increased stability of CtrA. Chloramphenicol chase experiments (Figure 5D and E) revealed that CtrA is indeed more stable in ∆citA cells than in WT cells, with the stability levels being similar to that of a non-degradable version of CtrA (ctrA::ctrA-M2) (Domian et al., 1997).
evidence: Stated in the results and supported by chloramphenicol chase data shown in Figure 5D and E.

claim: RNAP occupancy is increased at many CtrA-dependent promoters in citA cells compared to WT cells.
source: This quantification revealed an increase of RNAP occupancy at many, but not all, CtrA-dependent promoters in cells lacking CitA when compared with WT cells.
evidence: Stated in the results and supported by ChIP-Seq data shown in Figure 5F and G.

claim: The promoters with the highest change in RNAP abundance in citA cells are those activated by CtrA in G1-phase.
source: Interestingly, the promoters with the highest change in abundance of RNAP in citA cells when compared with WT cells are those that are activated by CtrA in G1-phase (Figure 5F, Figure 5—figure supplement 1D; Delaby et al., 2019; Fumeaux et al., 2014; Schrader et al., 2016).
evidence: Stated in the results and supported by ChIP-Seq data shown in Figure 5F and Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claim: CitA is present at a constant level throughout the cell cycle.
source: Immunoblotting experiments, using polyclonal antibodies to CitA, revealed that CitA is present at a constant level throughout the cell cycle (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Stated in the results and supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Spontaneous suppressor mutants of citA::Tn or ΔcitA have frameshift mutations in ptsP.
source: Whole-genome sequencing of two citA::Tn and one ∆citA suppressor mutant revealed a different frameshift mutation in the same domain of the PEP-phosphotransferase protein encoded by the ptsP gene (CCNA_00892) (Ronneau et al., 2016; Sanselicio et al., 2015).
evidence: Stated in the results based on whole-genome sequencing data.

claim: PtsP inhibits the hydrolase activity of SpoT.
source: PtsP resembles the first enzyme of a nitrogen-related PEP-phosphotransferase (PTS) protein homolog (EINtr in Enterobacteria) and was shown to inhibit the hydrolase activity of SpoT, the bifunctional synthase/hydrolase of the (p)ppGpp alarmone (Ronneau et al., 2016).
evidence: Stated in the results with supporting citation.

claim: Loss of (p)ppGpp production mitigates the effects caused by loss of CitA.
source: Importantly, the FACS profile of ∆ptsP citA::Tn or ∆spoT citA::Tn double mutant cells mirrors that of WT cells, indicating that loss of (p)ppGpp production indeed mitigates the effects caused by loss of CitA (Figure 6A), including the enhanced levels of CtrA ~P that are restored to WT levels in citA; ptsP double-mutant cells (Figure 5B, C, D and E).
evidence: Stated in the results and supported by FACS and immunoblotting data shown in Figure 6A and Figure 5B, C, D, and E.

claim: Quantification of (p)ppGpp in citA mutant cells grown in PYE did not reveal an increase compared to WT.
source: Quantification of radiolabeled (p)ppGpp extracted from WT and citA mutant cells grown in PYE did not reveal an increase in (p)ppGpp levels (Figure 6B), suggesting that inactivation of citA and the (p)ppGpp pathways converge on the same target.
evidence: Stated in the results and supported by TLC data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Inactivation of citA and the (p)ppGpp pathways converge on the same target.
source: Quantification of radiolabeled (p)ppGpp extracted from WT and citA mutant cells grown in PYE did not reveal an increase in (p)ppGpp levels (Figure 6B), suggesting that inactivation of citA and the (p)ppGpp pathways converge on the same target.
evidence: Stated as an inference in the results based on (p)ppGpp quantification data.

claim: CitA acts negatively on CtrA~P and this action depends on the presence of (p)ppGpp.
source: We conclude that CitA acts negatively on CtrA ~P and that this action depends on the presence of (p)ppGpp.
evidence: Stated as a conclusion in the results based on genetic and biochemical data.

claim: Ectopic induction of (p)ppGpp in WT cells delays the G1→S transition and prevents turnover of CtrA.
source: Ectopic induction of (p)ppGpp in WT cells delays the G1→S transition and prevents the concomitant turnover of CtrA.
evidence: Stated in the discussion based on cited literature.

claim: (p)ppGpp is required for the manifestation of the citA phenotype.
source: However, (p)ppGpp levels are not altered in the citA mutant, yet (p)ppGpp is absolutely required for the manifestation of the citA phenotype.
evidence: Stated in the discussion based on experimental data showing suppression by ΔspoT and ΔptsP.

claim: CitA and the (p)ppGpp pathways converge to cause an increase in active CtrA.
source: On the basis of these results, we propose that CitA and the (p)ppGpp pathways converge to cause an increase in active CtrA (Figure 6C).
evidence: Stated as a proposal in the discussion based on experimental data and illustrated in Figure 6C.

claim: (p)ppGpp is a well-known transcriptional target of RNAP.
source: Although we cannot exclude the hypothesis that CitA acts downstream of (p)ppGpp, a well-known transcriptional target of (p)ppGpp is RNAP (Hauryliuk et al., 2015).
evidence: Stated in the discussion with supporting citation.

claim: RNAP is a target of (p)ppGpp in alpha-proteobacteria.
source: RNAP also seems to be a target of (p)ppGpp in alpha-proteobacteria (Delaby et al., 2019; Wells and Long, 2003), suggesting that the effect of (p)ppGpp on CtrA is mediated by a change in transcription.
evidence: Stated in the discussion with supporting citations.

claim: The effect of (p)ppGpp on CtrA is mediated by a change in transcription.
source: RNAP also seems to be a target of (p)ppGpp in alpha-proteobacteria (Delaby et al., 2019; Wells and Long, 2003), suggesting that the effect of (p)ppGpp on CtrA is mediated by a change in transcription.
evidence: Stated as a suggestion in the discussion based on cited literature.

claim: Control of CtrA stability is mediated by the proteolytic adaptors CpdR, RcdA, and PopA.
source: As control of CtrA stability is mediated by the proteolytic adaptors CpdR, RcdA and PopA (Joshi and Chien, 2016), it is tempting to speculate that the citA mutation influences this pathway.
evidence: Stated in the discussion with supporting citation.

claim: The citA::Tn mutation was isolated as a suppressor from a ΔtipN ΔcpdR background.
source: However, the fact that the citA::Tn mutation was isolated as a suppressor from a ∆tipN ∆cpdR background already argues against this possibility.
evidence: Stated in the discussion based on the genetic screen results.

claim: Activities of CtrA-dependent transcriptional reporters are diminished in ΔpopA and ΔcpdR mutant cells relative to WT.
source: Moreover, we observed that the activities of the CtrA-dependent transcriptional reporters PpilA-lacZ and PhfsJ-lacZ are diminished in ∆popA and ∆cpdR mutant cells relative to those in WT cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E), whereas reporter activities in the citA mutant exceed WT levels.
evidence: Stated in the discussion and supported by β-galactosidase assay data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1E.

claim: CitA is perfectly positioned to integrate central energy metabolism with cell cycle transcriptional regulation by affecting CtrA.
source: By affecting CtrA, arguably the master regulator of the C. crescentus cell cycle, CitA is perfectly positioned to integrate central energy metabolism with cell cycle transcriptional regulation.
evidence: Stated in the discussion as an interpretation of the findings.

claim: The function of CitA in cell cycle control is unique to CitA and not shared by CitB or GltA.
source: This function is unique to CitA, as expression of the paralog CitB from C. crescentus or the GltA ortholog from E. coli in ∆citA cells does not restore cell cycle control, even though both enzymes exhibit efficient citrate synthase activity in an E. coli reporter system.
evidence: Stated in the discussion based on complementation experiments.

claim: The citA mutant phenotype is not simply caused by a metabolic deficiency of blocked citrate production.
source: Our finding that addition of glutamine does not rescue the developmental problem of a ∆citA strain and that metabolite extractions from citA mutant cells grown on PYE do not reveal a major perturbance in the levels of tricarboxylic acids, provide further support for the conclusion that the citA mutant phenotype is not simply caused by a metabolic deficiency of blocked citrate production.
evidence: Stated in the discussion based on glutamine supplementation and metabolomics data.

claim: Catalytically inactive CitA variants still confer cell cycle control functions.
source: Complementation analysis with catalytically inactive CitA variants revealed that they still confer cell cycle control functions.
evidence: Stated in the discussion based on complementation experiments with CitAH303W and CitAH303A.

claim: Other TCA cycle enzymes are essential for viability in C. crescentus.
source: Moreover, other TCA cycle enzymes are essential for viability in C. crescentus (Christen et al., 2011) Figure 3, presumably because TCA products are essential during growth on PYE.
evidence: Stated in the discussion with supporting citation and reference to Figure 3.

claim: The apparent redundancy in citrate synthase activities may have allowed the appropriation of CitA to control the cell cycle.
source: Thus, the apparent redundancy in citrate synthase activities may have allowed the appropriation of CitA to control the cell cycle, as a checkpoint regulator and 'moonlighting' or 'trigger' enzyme.
evidence: Stated in the discussion as an evolutionary interpretation.

claim: Other bacterial lineages also encode multiple citrate synthases.
source: Other bacterial lineages also encode multiple citrate synthases, and even within the Rhizobia, symbiotic relatives of C. crescentus, genera with three citA paralogs are often found (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Stated in the discussion and supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The GltA citrate synthase from Klebsiella pneumoniae is a virulence determinant required for replication in different organs.
source: Recently, the GltA citrate synthase from Klebsiella pneumoniae was identified as a virulence determinant (Vornhagen et al., 2019) that is required for replication in different organs, despite the presence of a GltA paralog in the genome.
evidence: Stated in the discussion with supporting citation.

claim: TCA cycle proteins have been implicated in conferring persister traits in Staphylococcus aureus cells.
source: In addition, TCA cycle proteins have been implicated in conferring persister (non-growing) traits in Staphylococcus aureus cells that protect them against bacteriocidal antibiotics (Zalis et al., 2019).
evidence: Stated in the discussion with supporting citation.

claim: B. subtilis cells that lack citrate synthase sporulate poorly.
source: B. subtilis cells that lack citrate synthase sporulate poorly (Ireton et al., 1995) and a citrate synthase mutant of Streptomyces coelicolor is impaired in aerial mycelium formation (Viollier et al., 2001).
evidence: Stated in the discussion with supporting citation.

claim: A citrate synthase mutant of Streptomyces coelicolor is impaired in aerial mycelium formation.
source: B. subtilis cells that lack citrate synthase sporulate poorly (Ireton et al., 1995) and a citrate synthase mutant of Streptomyces coelicolor is impaired in aerial mycelium formation (Viollier et al., 2001).
evidence: Stated in the discussion with supporting citation.

claim: In S. coelicolor, while the growth defect of the citrate synthase mutant on minimal medium was suppressed by glutamate addition, development remains perturbed.
source: Importantly, while the growth defect of the citrate synthase mutant in S. coelicolor on minimal medium was suppressed by the addition of glutamate, development remains perturbed.
evidence: Stated in the discussion with supporting citation.

claim: Central metabolic enzymes serve as ideal checkpoint mechanisms that couple developmental gene expression to central energy metabolism.
source: Thus, developmental events in bacteria may be controlled by switches, and central metabolic enzymes serve as ideal checkpoint mechanisms that couple developmental gene expression to central energy metabolism.
evidence: Stated in the discussion as a general conclusion.

claim: In Saccharomyces cerevisiae, CIT1 is located in the mitochondria where it participates in the TCA cycle.
source: Eukaryotic cells, such as those of Saccharomyces cerevisiae, restrict citrate synthase paralogs to different compartments of the cell. CIT1 is located in the mitochondria where it participates in the TCA cycle, while CIT2 is located in the peroxisome, where it acts in the glyoxylate cycle (Kim et al., 1986; Rosenkrantz et al., 1986).
evidence: Stated in the discussion with supporting citations.

claim: In Saccharomyces cerevisiae, CIT2 is located in the peroxisome where it acts in the glyoxylate cycle.
source: Eukaryotic cells, such as those of Saccharomyces cerevisiae, restrict citrate synthase paralogs to different compartments of the cell. CIT1 is located in the mitochondria where it participates in the TCA cycle, while CIT2 is located in the peroxisome, where it acts in the glyoxylate cycle (Kim et al., 1986; Rosenkrantz et al., 1986).
evidence: Stated in the discussion with supporting citations.

claim: In Podospora anserina, a citrate synthase mutant strain exhibits a developmental phenotype that impairs meiosis independently of its catalytic activity.
source: In Podospora anserina, a citrate synthase mutant strain exhibits a developmental phenotype that impairs meiosis independently of its catalytic citrate synthase activity (Ruprich-Robert et al., 2002), reminiscent of our finding highlighting alternate functions of citrate synthases in cell cycle control of another domain of life.
evidence: Stated in the discussion with supporting citation.

claim: The cellular redox potential changes as a function of the C. crescentus cell cycle.
source: Evidence has been provided that the cellular redox potential changes as a function of the C. crescentus cell cycle (Narayanan et al., 2015), and a recent study revealed that glutathione and many unknown metabolites fluctuate in accordance with the cell cycle (Hartl et al., 2020).
evidence: Stated in the discussion with supporting citation.

claim: Glutathione and many unknown metabolites fluctuate in accordance with the C. crescentus cell cycle.
source: Evidence has been provided that the cellular redox potential changes as a function of the C. crescentus cell cycle (Narayanan et al., 2015), and a recent study revealed that glutathione and many unknown metabolites fluctuate in accordance with the cell cycle (Hartl et al., 2020).
evidence: Stated in the discussion with supporting citation.

claim: KidO is an NADH-binding protein present in G1-phase and during cell constriction.
source: The oxidoreductase homolog KidO is an NADH-binding protein that is present in the G1-phase and during cell constriction.
evidence: Stated in the discussion based on cited literature.

claim: KidO is bifunctional, acting as a cell division inhibitor that binds FtsZ and as a negative regulator of the CtrA activation pathway.
source: KidO is bifunctional, acting as cell division inhibitor that binds FtsZ and as a negative regulator of the CtrA activation pathway (Radhakrishnan et al., 2010).
evidence: Stated in the discussion with supporting citation.

claim: GdhZ is a glutamate dehydrogenase whose activity is modulated by glutamate and NADH.
source: Interestingly, another division regulator that functions as a moonlighting enzyme and that is degraded in a ClpXP and CpdR-dependent manner has been identified: the glutamate dehydrogenase GdhZ whose activity is modulated by glutamate and NADH (Beaufay et al., 2015).
evidence: Stated in the discussion with supporting citation.

claim: GdhZ is degraded in a ClpXP and CpdR-dependent manner.
source: Interestingly, another division regulator that functions as a moonlighting enzyme and that is degraded in a ClpXP and CpdR-dependent manner has been identified: the glutamate dehydrogenase GdhZ whose activity is modulated by glutamate and NADH (Beaufay et al., 2015).
evidence: Stated in the discussion with supporting citation.

claim: C. crescentus integrates cell cycle control with central cellular metabolism at multiple levels using different checkpoint regulators derived from metabolic enzymes.
source: The fact that KidO and GdhZ, two NAD(H) binding proteins, and CitA, an active citrate synthase, execute cell cycle control functions, indicates that C. crescentus, and probably other bacteria, integrate cell cycle control with central cellular metabolism (at multiple levels) using different checkpoint regulators derived from metabolic enzymes.
evidence: Stated in the discussion as a conclusion based on the collective evidence.

claim: The moonlighting functions of KidO, GdhZ, and CitA are not apparent by analysis of their primary structure.
source: The moonlighting functions of KidO, GdhZ and CitA are not apparent by analysis of their primary structure.
evidence: Stated in the discussion as an observation.

claim: GdhZ was discovered as an interaction partner of FtsZ in a yeast two-hybrid screen.
source: Although GdhZ was discovered as an interaction partner of FtsZ in a yeast two-hybrid screen (Beaufay et al., 2015), the genes encoding KidO and CitA both emerged from a forward genetic selection for cell cycle mutants that restore activity of the CtrA-regulated promoter PpilA that fires in G1-phase (Radhakrishnan et al., 2010).
evidence: Stated in the discussion with supporting citation.

claim: The genes encoding KidO and CitA emerged from a forward genetic selection for cell cycle mutants that restore PpilA activity.
source: Although GdhZ was discovered as an interaction partner of FtsZ in a yeast two-hybrid screen (Beaufay et al., 2015), the genes encoding KidO and CitA both emerged from a forward genetic selection for cell cycle mutants that restore activity of the CtrA-regulated promoter PpilA that fires in G1-phase (Radhakrishnan et al., 2010).
evidence: Stated in the discussion with supporting citation.

claim: CtrA targeted promoters include those controlling expression of envelope and developmental functions as well as metabolic functions.
source: As CtrA targeted promoters include not only those controlling expression of envelope and developmental functions, but also those controlling metabolic functions (Fiebig et al., 2014; Fumeaux et al., 2014; Laub et al., 2000), it is appealing to speculate that the molecular and genetic interplay between metabolism and cell cycle control is much more profound than anticipated, at least in C. crescentus and related bacteria.
evidence: Stated in the discussion with supporting citations.

claim: The molecular and genetic interplay between metabolism and cell cycle control may be much more profound than anticipated in C. crescentus and related bacteria.
source: As CtrA targeted promoters include not only those controlling expression of envelope and developmental functions, but also those controlling metabolic functions (Fiebig et al., 2014; Fumeaux et al., 2014; Laub et al., 2000), it is appealing to speculate that the molecular and genetic interplay between metabolism and cell cycle control is much more profound than anticipated, at least in C. crescentus and related bacteria.
evidence: Stated in the discussion as speculation based on the findings.
